title: Evaluating a Deterministic Validator Plus Single‑Iteration Repair Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configurations
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (N=300 paired intent→configuration tasks; preregistration id cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1) to evaluate whether a minimal guarded pipeline—single‑shot LLM generation (declared model: gpt-5-mini) followed by a frozen deterministic configuration validator and at most one automated repair iteration—reduces first‑pass misconfiguration relative to plain single‑shot generation. Execution completed 600 episodes and used 301 model calls. Observed outcomes: baseline = 299/300 valid (99.667%); guarded = 300/300 valid (100.0%); paired counts n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; absolute paired difference = 0.0033333; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). The single permitted automated repair corrected the sole invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1; Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]). The preregistered planning assumption used for power calculations (planned baseline pass rate = 0.40) was contradicted by the observed near‑ceiling baseline, removing statistical headroom for the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction target. We report preregistered design choices, execution accounting, confirmatory statistics, an artifact‑grounded sensitivity bound tied to the observed contingency counts, and reproducibility primitives. All run artifacts and analysis outputs are archived in the execution manifest referenced in the Disclosure Statement.

sections.introduction: Translating operator intent into device configuration is a central NetOps task. Large language models (LLMs) can accelerate intent→configuration synthesis but produce probabilistic outputs that risk omission, misordering, or unsafe commands. Hybrid workflows that pair probabilistic generators with deterministic validators and bounded repair loops are widely advocated as operational floor‑safety nets, yet rigorous, preregistered evaluations that quantify first‑pass misconfiguration reductions under controlled sampling semantics are scarce. We therefore preregistered and executed a narrowly focused paired experiment to evaluate whether a minimal guarded pipeline—(1) a single shared LLM candidate per task, (2) a frozen deterministic validator that canonicalizes and statically checks constraints, and (3) at most one automated repair attempt when violations are reported—reduces first‑pass misconfiguration relative to plain single‑shot generation. The Introduction closes by stating the research question and contributions. Research question: Can this minimal guarded pipeline reduce first‑pass misconfiguration rate relative to plain single‑shot generation under a controlled paired design? Contributions: (i) a preregistered paired experiment with deterministic seed generation and archived per‑task artifacts; (ii) confirmatory statistics and artifact‑grounded diagnostics; (iii) explicit accounting of a preregistration planning assumption that materially affected interpretability; (iv) practical, artifact‑grounded recommendations for future NetOps confirmatory evaluations.
sections.related_work: Recent demonstrations and surveys document growing interest in LLMs for intent‑driven configuration and NetOps automation, while also highlighting failure modes (misordering, omission, hallucination) and the value of verifier/validator integrations [10.1002/nem.2313; 10.36227/techrxiv.176784505.56675782/v1]. Work in adjacent domains (medical QA, code repair) shows that verifier‑assisted or RAG‑augmented pipelines reduce factual errors and improve grounding, motivating guarded designs for NetOps [10.2139/ssrn.6608518]. Deterministic verification techniques (e.g., header‑space and specification checks) provide algorithmic foundations for static validators that can check reachability and policy constraints without live execution [10.1145/3098822.3098834]. Survey and policy work emphasize auditability and human oversight as open challenges [10.6028/nist.ai.100-2e2023]. Our study sits at the intersection of these strands by executing a preregistered paired evaluation that directly measures first‑pass validity under an explicit validator+repair floor.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and hypotheses: We preregistered study cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1 before observing outcomes. Confirmatory hypotheses: H1 — guarded pipeline reduces first‑pass misconfiguration rate by ≥50% (relative) vs single‑shot generation; H2 — one or fewer automated repair iterations recover ≥75% of initially invalid configurations. The preregistration explicitly used a planning assumption baseline pass rate = 0.40 to translate target relative effect into required N; that numeric planning assumption is central to statistical interpretation and is reported here. Important: the observed baseline (299/300) contradicts the planning assumption and therefore removes inferential headroom needed to test H1 as preregistered; H1 is not supported (nor meaningfully testable) given the observed near‑ceiling baseline—see Results and Discussion for artifact‑grounded explanation.

Design and sampling semantics: The design is paired within‑task with a frozen deterministic seed list of 300 tasks. For each seed we used the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics: the generator produced one configuration (shared candidate) that served as the baseline response and as the starting point for the guarded arm's validation and possible repair. Planned episodes = 600; initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1; maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1. The shared‑candidate pairing was chosen to emulate operational remediation of a single proposed plan (higher ecological validity) but increases within‑pair correlation and reduces expected discordant pairs relative to independent‑draws designs; this tradeoff was preregistered and informed the power calculations.

Model and sampling determinism: The declared generation model in the execution contract was gpt-5-mini. The archived model configuration records that the sampling temperature parameter was unset (temperature = null) in execution/model_configuration.json; this artifact is authoritative for the run configuration (see execution/model_configuration.json in the execution manifest). Because provider default sampling semantics are outside this archived artifact and were not fixed in the preregistration, sampling determinism is unspecified in the experiment: we do not assert deterministic token‑level generation from the provider. This uncertainty in sampling determinism affects reproducibility of token‑for‑token outputs but does not change the paired design’s logic because both arms used the same shared candidate per pair (shared_initial_candidate semantics). Analysts reproducing the run should rely on the archived execution/model_configuration.json for the exact recorded generation parameters.

Validator, canonicalization, and scoring semantics: The frozen deterministic validator canonicalized generated responses to a normalized AST and applied static checks derived from task workflow policies (must_be_down_for_fields, final_group_constraints, minimum_active_in_groups, required_sequence). The scoring rule was full intent‑constraint validation: success requires that the validator's normalized_configuration satisfies the task required_sequence and expected_final_state and that no protected/forbidden touches occurred. The validator trace includes normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_codes, repair_applied flags; these structured traces triggered the repair adapter and were the basis for per‑task scoring and downstream analysis.

Repair adapter: The preregistered repair adapter is invoked only when the validator reports violations on the shared candidate. It is limited to a single automated repair attempt per episode and aims to minimally edit the candidate to remove reported violations while preserving original plan structure where allowed. Post‑repair candidate is revalidated by the same deterministic validator.

Primary estimand and analysis: The primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. The preregistered primary test is the exact McNemar two‑sided test at α=0.05 on paired binary outcomes; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CIs were preregistered with 10,000 resamples and seed = 1729. The preregistration also specified sensitivity treatments for failed provider calls and deterministic contamination detection rules. All preregistered elements and the execution manifest are archived.
sections.results:
Execution accounting (artifact‑derived): Planned episodes = 600; completed episodes = 600; complete pairs analyzed = 300. Model calls used = 301 (300 shared initial generations + 1 repair invocation). No provider or infrastructure failures occurred under the preregistered retry policy; no deterministic exclusions for contamination were triggered.

Primary outcomes (archived counts): Baseline_success_count = 299/300 (99.667%); Guarded_success_count = 300/300 (100.0%). The archived paired contingency (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0. Confirmatory inference (preregistered): exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00 on the observed contingency; absolute paired difference = (n10 − n01)/300 = 1/300 ≈ 0.0033333. The paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the absolute paired difference = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, bootstrap seed = 1729), as computed from the archived analysis artifacts.

Why p = 1.00 (artifact‑grounded explanation): The exact McNemar test conditions on the observed discordant total (n10 + n01). With only one discordant pair (n10 + n01 = 1) the test’s conditional sampling distribution offers no possibility of a small two‑sided p‑value for a large preregistered absolute effect because there are insufficient discordant outcomes; this directly explains p = 1.00 for our observed pattern. The archived paired_contingency_table.csv and the bootstrap parameters (seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000) are the authoritative artifacts for these numbers. Put differently, the observed discordant count imposes a hard upper bound on resolvable absolute paired difference equal to 1/300 ≈ 0.00333; the preregistered target of a ≥50% relative reduction (mapped from a planning baseline = 0.40) would have required O(90) net discordant pairs favoring guarded outputs for detection at the planned power.

Repair outcomes (H2): The single allowed automated repair corrected the sole invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1). The conditional repair estimate is therefore 1.00 with Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0], reflecting extreme imprecision because only one initially invalid case was observed. Per‑task validator traces (normalized_configuration, violation_codes, repair_applied) for every episode are archived and are the primary evidence for these counts.
sections.discussion:
Artifact‑grounded interpretation and design lessons. The run’s artifacts show that when baseline error prevalence is near ceiling, preregistered large relative effects cannot be tested: the observed discordant count (1) mathematically constrains resolvable absolute differences to 1/300. This is an empirical and design lesson traceable to the archived paired contingency and the execution manifest. The preregistered shared_initial_candidate pairing emulates operational remediation of a single plan but increases within‑pair correlation and reduces expected discordance; future studies must jointly consider pairing semantics and baseline prevalence in power planning.

Practical recommendations grounded in artifacts: (1) Calibrate task difficulty or adversarially augment tasks to produce a nontrivial baseline failure prevalence (or target a preregistered discordant‑pair count) so conditional repair and paired differences can be estimated with desired precision. Use deterministic task generators with adjustable difficulty knobs and record them in the manifest. (2) Explicitly preregister pairing semantics, repair budgets, and how emulator or runtime validation (if used) maps to success/failure; incorporate these choices into power/sample size arithmetic. (3) When runtime consequences are relevant, add an emulation/simulation stage and preregister how emulator outcomes feed the success criterion; static validators do not capture dynamic control‑plane effects. These recommendations are actionable because task difficulty fields, validator violation codes, and the paired contingency table are present in the archived artifacts.

Construct and external validity: Our validator performed deterministic static checks and canonicalization rather than executing configurations in devices or emulation; therefore results are conditional on validator coverage and do not measure runtime convergence or transient reachability. The synthetic task bank and constrained vendor templates enumerated in the manifest limit external generalization to production topologies and vendor heterogeneity. Repair effectiveness remains imprecisely estimated because only one initial failure occurred; larger numbers of initial failures are required to precisely estimate P(repair succeeds | initial failure).

Reproducibility and auditability: The run demonstrates the value of archival primitives: per‑task inputs, normalized responses, validator traces, repair prompts/responses, the paired contingency table, and analysis code allow recomputation of reported counts and intervals. Analysts should consult the execution manifest and analysis artifacts (e.g., execution/model_configuration.json; analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv; analysis/condition_summary.csv) for authoritative details.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired experiment (N=300 pairs) comparing single‑shot LLM generation (gpt-5-mini) to a guarded pipeline consisting of a frozen deterministic validator and a single automated repair iteration. The archived artifacts show baseline 299/300 valid and guarded 300/300 valid; the single permitted automated repair corrected the lone invalid baseline output. However, the preregistered planning assumption (baseline pass rate = 0.40) diverged from observed data (near‑ceiling baseline), removing statistical headroom to detect the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction. Future confirmatory NetOps evaluations should (a) calibrate task difficulty or adversarially augment tasks to ensure sufficient initial failures or target discordant counts, (b) explicitly preregister pairing semantics and repair budgets and incorporate them into power computations, and (c) include emulation when runtime semantic claims are intended. All raw outputs, validator traces, repair traces, the execution manifest, and analysis artifacts are archived and enumerated in the Disclosure Statement to permit reproduction of the reported counts and intervals.

limitations: Synthetic task bank and constrained vendor‑template scope limit external validity to broad production environments.
Single LLM (gpt-5-mini) and a single validator implementation restrict generality across model families and validator designs.

The preregistered power plan assumed a baseline pass rate = 0.40; the observed baseline (299/300) contradicted that assumption and removed headroom to detect the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction.
Sampling semantics (shared_initial_candidate) reused the same initial candidate across paired arms, increasing within‑pair correlation and reducing discordant pairs available to McNemar inference.

Validation used deterministic configuration/constraint checks rather than full dynamic emulation of runtime semantic effects; actual runtime consequences of configurations were not executed and remain unmeasured.

H2 repair‑success evidence is based on a single initially invalid case (1/1 → 100%), yielding a wide Clopper‑Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]; larger counts of initial failures are required to estimate repair effectiveness precisely.
